title: PolitiFact Says Project 2025 Does Not Propose Ending Same-Sex Marriage
description_short: PolitiFact Says Project 2025 Does Not Propose Ending Same-Sex Marriage
description_medium: The linked PolitiFact summary says Project 2025 does not propose ending same-sex marriage. It describes the plan as favoring heterosexual, two-parent families and supporting protections for faith-based grant recipients that oppose same-sex marriage. The supplied material discusses proposals and possible effects; it does not describe a federal program to annul existing marriages or revoke their recognition.
description_long: The linked PolitiFact fact-check addresses claims that Project 2025 would end same-sex marriage. The supplied account says the fact-check rejects that claim: it does not describe a proposal to annul existing marriages or remove federal recognition. Instead, the summary says the plan prioritizes heterosexual, two-parent families and includes proposed protections for faith-based organizations receiving federal grants if they object to same-sex marriage. The packet notes that other proposals could limit LGBTQ protections, but it gives no details of a federal mechanism for ending marriage equality. These are policy proposals and an analysis of possible effects, not an implemented federal annulment program. The description therefore distinguishes the plan’s family-policy preferences and grant provisions from the unsupported claims that Trump eliminated marriage recognition or enabled states to void existing marriages. No completed Trump administration action, court ruling, or loss of legal status is asserted.
notes: The supplied fact-check summary says Project 2025 does not propose ending same-sex marriage, while describing family-policy and faith-based grant proposals. The prior focused request to the linked PolitiFact page returned HTTP 403; the description is limited to the supplied summary and does not claim implementation.

title: Brian Murphy’s Complaint Alleged DHS Officials Pressed Him to Change Threat Assessments
description_short: Brian Murphy’s Complaint Alleged DHS Officials Pressed Him to Change Threat Assessments
description_medium: In a September 2020 whistleblower complaint, DHS intelligence official Brian Murphy alleged that Deputy Secretary Ken Cuccinelli pressed him to downplay white-supremacist threats and emphasize left-wing groups such as Antifa. Murphy said he refused and alleged Acting Secretary Chad Wolf later echoed the requests. The packet supplies no official finding that verifies the alleged instructions or edits.
description_long: DHS intelligence official Brian Murphy filed a whistleblower complaint in September 2020 concerning threat assessments produced during the Trump administration. According to the supplied account, Murphy alleged that then-Deputy Secretary Ken Cuccinelli asked him in May to reduce the prominence of white-supremacist threats and emphasize threats from left-wing groups, including Antifa. Murphy said he declined to make the requested changes. He also alleged that Acting Secretary Chad Wolf later echoed the requests and that an assessment was completed without his approval after he refused edits. The complaint reportedly covered other intelligence disputes, and Murphy said he was reassigned in August. These are allegations by the complainant, not findings established in the packet. The linked TrumpFile timeline returned HTTP 202 without readable text, and no inspector-general report, congressional finding, or final complaint disposition is supplied. Still missing is authoritative evidence establishing whether officials issued the alleged instructions, whether the final assessments were changed, and how investigators resolved the complaint.
notes: The linked TrumpFile source returned HTTP 202 without readable text. The packet attributes the requested assessment changes to Murphy’s complaint but supplies no inspector-general report, congressional finding, or final disposition. Those findings and the final assessment text remain missing.

title: TrumpFile Post Claims Trump Never Planned to Win the November 2024 Election
description_short: TrumpFile Post Claims Trump Never Planned to Win the November 2024 Election
description_medium: An August 2024 TrumpFile post asserted that Donald Trump never planned to win the November election, but the supplied synopsis includes no supporting quotation. A later Axios report described campaign contingency planning for either outcome and said Trump expected to win while acknowledging he could lose. That later report does not establish his private intent.
description_long: The title of an August 2024 TrumpFile post asserted that Donald Trump never intended to win the November election, but the supplied synopsis provides no quotation or evidence supporting that conclusion. The linked TrumpFile page was inaccessible in the source pass. A separate Axios report published on November 4 described a campaign email planning for both possible outcomes, including winding down payroll if Trump lost and moving some staff into transition or inauguration work if he won. Axios also reported that Trump expected to win while privately acknowledging that he could lose. Contingency planning for either outcome does not show that a campaign lacked an intention to win, and the Axios report postdates the August post. The material supports distinguishing routine election planning from a claim about a candidate’s private intent. A contemporaneous statement or document supporting that intent claim is still needed; until then, the assertion remains attributed to the post rather than established as fact.
notes: Focused read of the linked Axios article returned HTTP 403. The supplied account describes contingency planning and an expectation of victory, which do not establish the August post’s claim about intent. Still missing is a contemporaneous statement or document that supports the claim.

title: FCC Approves Nexstar–TEGNA Merger as States Challenge Its Legality
description_short: FCC Approves Nexstar–TEGNA Merger as States Challenge Its Legality
description_medium: The linked TrumpFile report says the FCC and Justice Department approved the Nexstar–TEGNA merger on March 19, 2026, with six station divestitures and a combined reach of 54.5% of U.S. households. It reports that eight states sued, alleging the deal exceeded a federal reach limit. The packet supplies no final ruling or Trump-specific action behind the approval.
description_long: The linked TrumpFile report says the Federal Communications Commission and Justice Department approved Nexstar’s merger with TEGNA on March 19, 2026. It reports that the combined company would own 259 television stations and reach 54.5% of U.S. households after agreeing to divest six stations. The article says eight states sued, alleging that the transaction exceeded the 39% household-reach limit. Colorado Attorney General Phil Weiser warned that consolidation could reduce media diversity and raise costs; Nexstar’s chair and CEO Perry Sook is also named. These details describe regulatory approval and a pending legal challenge, not a final judicial determination that the deal was illegal. The separate linked CBS story concerns a Disney/ABC licensing dispute and does not resolve the Nexstar–TEGNA case. Neither supplied source documents a Trump order or personal action behind the approval. A final court disposition and evidence of a Trump-specific connection remain missing.
notes: The focused TrumpFile source reports approval, divestitures, reach figures, and an eight-state challenge, but no final ruling that the merger was illegal. The CBS link concerns another FCC matter. Still missing is a final legal disposition and any documented Trump-specific action.
